name: PT Central Omega Resources Tbk

frontmatter.title: Central Omega Resources: a long reserve, a short licence
frontmatter.summary: Central Omega Resources mines nickel ore in Sulawesi and sells it to domestic smelters inside Indonesia's RKAB quota system. We cut to HOLD with a Rp652 target, a 3.6% total return on the Rp700 price. The revision is about the licence, not the ore body: our DCF now stops at the last granted permit, in 2032, and the reserve beyond that date is an extension option we do not pay for.
thesis: Ore economics are the whole story: a cash cost of US$11.2 a tonne before royalty against an ore price of US$34.4 a tonne leaves a 45.5% EBITDA margin at the deck's nickel price, and the cost is contractor-borne rather than fixed.

We value only what the company is licensed to mine. The residual reserve is 89,306 kt, but the three producing IUPs expire in December 2027, April 2031 and March 2032, so the DCF stops at the last of them and produces Rp593 a share. No source discloses an extension application.

The market is already paying for more nickel than the deck assumes: at Rp700 the reverse DCF implies US$19,841/t a tonne, above the house through-cycle price, so the price is carrying both the deck's metal and part of the extension option.
Cash returns have restarted and are funded: net cash on the balance sheet, a payout of 69.0% of earnings and a dividend yield of 10.4% on our numbers.
The bear case is policy, not geology: a hard 2027 RKAB cut caps volumes and takes the value to Rp511, below the current price, which is why the rating is not BUY.

catalysts.event: Nine-month 2026 results and the volume run-rate against the RKAB quota
December HPM nickel ore reference price and the royalty band it sets
2027 RKAB approval; the government has signalled tighter nickel quotas
Konawe (BKA) IUP expires in December 2027: any extension application should be visible in the FY2026 annual report
FY2026 audited accounts and the final dividend proposal at the annual meeting

blocks.text: PT Central Omega Resources is a nickel ore miner with producing contract areas in Central and Southeast Sulawesi, a suspended ferronickel smelter and a limestone quarry it bought to supply the surrounding industrial parks. It sells ore, not metal, into a domestic market where the government sets the annual production quota and a monthly reference price. That makes it a leveraged play on three variables: the nickel price, transmitted through the HPM ore formula; the annual RKAB quota, which decides how many tonnes it may sell; and the mining licence, which decides for how many years it may sell at all. We cut to HOLD with a target of Rp652, a 3.6% total return on the Rp700 price [S2, S3, S11].

The revision is entirely about the third variable. Our earlier valuation discounted a reserve life of nearly three decades. The reserve is real — 89,306 kt of residual limonite and saprolite at the June 2026 balance-sheet date — but the company is not licensed for three decades: the Konawe permit expires in December 2027, the Morowali permit in April 2031 and the Lambolo permit in March 2032, and the blocks they cover hold almost all of that reserve [S3]. We now discount cash flow only to the last granted expiry, prorating any year in which a permit lapses mid-year, and the value falls to Rp593 a share. Everything after March 2032 is an extension application we neither assume nor pay for.

The operating case is unchanged and still good. A tonne of ore costs about US$11.2 to produce before royalty and sells for US$34.4 at the deck's nickel price, which is why FY2025 EBITDA reached 659.4 IDR billion on 1,576.2 IDR billion of sales [S2]. What has changed is how long that cash flow runs.

The cross-checks now disagree in the other direction. The peer-median EV/EBITDA multiple gives Rp971 per share, above the DCF, because the peers it is struck from hold licences that run longer than this company's — an earnings multiple cannot see a permit expiry that lands inside the seventh year. A book-value cross-check gives Rp309, which we weight lightly: a contractor-operated miner with a return on equity of 55.1% is not a book-value business [S2]. The weighted target of Rp652 sits above the DCF, carried by those two cross-checks, because the licence-limited primary value is lower than what an earnings multiple struck on longer-lived peers will pay.

What the market is paying for is visible in the reverse DCF. At Rp700 the share price implies a nickel price of US$19,841/t a tonne, above the house deck's through-cycle assumption and above the November spot print. The market is therefore not disputing the ore body, and it is not pricing a nickel collapse either: it is paying the deck's metal price plus a slice of the extension option that our base case refuses to assume. That is a defensible thing to pay for, and it is why we are at HOLD rather than SELL [S10, S12].

Two things would change our mind. A disclosed extension application, or a licence granted past 2032, would add value that is not in our number and would move the target toward the multiple cross-check. A 2027 RKAB set below the 2026 revision would move us to the bear case even at today's price.

Nickel has become an Indonesian policy market. The country supplies most of the world's mined nickel, the government manages volumes through annual company work plans, and the reference price for ore is set monthly by the ministry. Ore miners sit upstream of the smelters that turn saprolite into nickel pig iron and limonite into mixed hydroxide for batteries. Because the ore price is administratively derived rather than freely negotiated, a miner's revenue is a function of the metal price and a formula, while its cost is a function of diesel, labour, contractors and the strip ratio. The result is a business that looks like a commodity producer but trades on regulatory signals.

Central Omega Resources operates two nickel mining concessions and a limestone quarry, and it owns a ferronickel smelter that has been idle since 2022. The company is listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange under the basic materials sector and is controlled by PT Jinsheng Mining, which held 65.7% of the shares after its October 2026 purchase and states that it will keep control; the remainder is the free float [S6, S4]. The group runs a workforce in the low hundreds, most of them at the mine sites rather than at the Jakarta head office [S0].

The revenue mix is almost entirely nickel ore. In FY2025 nickel ore sales produced 1,520 IDR bn IDR billion and limestone produced 56.5 IDR bn IDR billion out of total revenue of 1,576.2 IDR billion, so the ore business is effectively the company [S2]. Limestone is a by-product of the same mining district: the company acquired PT Afit Lintas Jaya, which holds a limestone production licence in North Morowali, and sells quicklime to the smelters around the industrial park [S4]. The ferronickel smelter, held through the CORII subsidiary in which the group owns a majority stake, was designed in two phases with a capacity measured in hundreds of thousands of tonnes a year; the first phase was built and operated, the second was diverted into a battery-grade nickel study that has not been sanctioned, and the furnaces have not produced since 2022 because of coke supply and cost [S3, S4].

Volumes tell the growth story and its limits. Nickel ore sales rose from 1,269 kt kt in FY2023 to 2,598 kt kt in FY2024 and 3,029 kt kt in FY2025, while production reached 2,929 kt kt, effectively the RKAB target for the year [S4]. The 2025 work plan allowed 2,950 kt of ore and sales ran ahead of production, drawing on stockpiles [S4]. The constraint on further growth is the annual quota, not the plant: the company has said its 2026 plan is to lift output within whatever quota it is granted [S4]. No company-level 2026-2032 work plan appears in the archive, so we plan no more than the 2,950 kt permit the company disclosed for 2025, and the sales figure above the production line is stockpile draw rather than a repeatable run-rate [S3, S4].

The reserve statement is the asset that matters, and it needs restating properly. The annual report puts total limonite and saprolite reserves at a round figure of ninety-three million tonnes in a single MD&A sentence, with no unit, grade or classification and no reserve table anywhere in the report; the interim accounts carry the real table, by block and by licence, showing a total reserve of 108,012 kt and residual reserves of 89,306 kt at the June 2026 balance-sheet date after production to date [S3, S4]. We model the residual figure, not the round number. At the planned sales rate the residual is a reserve life of nearly three decades, but the licensed life is shorter: the Konawe permit runs to December 2027, the Morowali permit to April 2031 and the Lambolo permit to March 2032, and the Konawe blocks that fall away first are a small part of the total while almost all the rest sits under the two later permits [S3]. We searched the annual report, the interim accounts and the press to November 2026 and found no extension application and no statement of the statutory basis on which an extension would be granted, so the model values the licensed term and treats the reserve beyond March 2032 as an option rather than an asset. The separate MPR Kupang exploration permit, which covers nickel and copper to June 2031, is excluded from the valuation entirely as an unsourced option rather than a reserve: we mention it so the exclusion is visible, not because we have a value for it [S3].

Customers are the smelters in the Morowali and Konawe industrial parks, and the receivable book shows how concentrated that is. The list has changed shape in the first half: Sino Indo Nickel is still the largest debtor, followed by Shanxi Minmetals and Ivoryline Investment, but three new names — Karunia Permai Sentosa, Eco Energi Perkasa and Sulawesi Mining Investment — came onto the book between December and June and together make up more than a third of the gross balance, while Five Star General Resources, Obi Nickel Cobalt and Megah Surya Pertiwi are smaller [S3]. The audited accounts classify every one of these debtors as a third party, and the related-party note discloses only key-management compensation, so this is counterparty concentration among independent smelters rather than an affiliated-sales problem — but it is concentration all the same, and it is what the impairment allowance is for [S2, S3].

The strategy is deliberately narrow: keep the mine running at the quota limit, sell limestone to the park, keep the smelter option alive at minimal cost, and pay out cash. There is no funded expansion, no acquisition programme and no new smelter line in the plan, which is why capital expenditure was only 1.0 IDR bn IDR billion in FY2025 [S2]. Management's stated ambition is to move further downstream into battery raw materials, but that remains a study rather than a commitment [S4].

Indonesia is the supply side of the nickel market. The energy minister puts the country's share of global supply at roughly two thirds, and the same official describes global capacity as oversupplying consumption by a wide margin [S10]. That mismatch is why the government has spent two years managing volumes through the RKAB process rather than leaving the market to clear. The 2026 quota was revised upwards in October but remains below the volume actually produced in 2025, and the 2027 quota is under evaluation with an explicit threat of a cut [S11, S12].

The policy has started to work. CRU told a Jakarta conference in November that Indonesia's supply restrictions had helped balance the market in 2026, in contrast to the large surplus that had been expected at the start of the year, and it identified the 2027 quota as the single biggest determinant of the global balance [S9]. Inventories remain the problem: the ministry is watching metal stocks sitting in London and Shanghai exchange warehouses as it decides the 2027 number [S11]. The metal price has responded to the tightening, with nickel trading near US$16,324/t a tonne against a house through-cycle assumption of US$17,500/t [S0].

For an ore miner the transmission mechanism is the HPM reference price. The ministry publishes a monthly ore price derived from the metal price and the ore's grade, and the royalty follows it. Under PP 19/2025 the nickel ore royalty is banded on the reference nickel price: 14.0% while the reference nickel price is below the lower threshold of the schedule, rising progressively to a top rate of nineteen per cent once the reference price passes the upper threshold [S13, S14, S15]. The royalty is therefore not a stable share of revenue; it is a variable that takes a larger slice of the ore price exactly when prices rise, and it is modelled that way here: the deck's through-cycle price sits in the bottom band through the licensed horizon and the rate edges up in the final two years as the price path crosses the threshold [S14, S15].

Competitive positioning rests on cost and on the licence, not on brand or scale. The company is a small producer against the integrated groups: its 3,029.3 kt of sales is a rounding error against a national quota measured in hundreds of millions of tonnes [S11]. What it has is a low cash cost, because mining is contractor-operated and the ore is close to the smelters that buy it, and a reserve that is large relative to its production. What it does not have is pricing power: the HPM formula and the quota set both the price and the volume, so the company is a price-taker on both axes [S14, S12].

The five forces are unusually clear. Buyer power is high and concentrated in a handful of independent smelters, several of them newly added to the receivable book in 2026 [S2, S3]. Supplier power sits with the contractors and with diesel, though the contractor structure passes fuel through rather than fixing it [S2]. New entry is controlled by the RKAB and by the licence moratorium the government is now discussing, which protects incumbents [S10]. Substitution runs the other way: limonite can go to high-pressure acid leach plants and saprolite to rotary kilns, so the same ore body serves both routes. Rivalry among RKAB holders is muted by the quota, which is the point of the policy.

The moat, in short, is a regulatory rent rather than an economic one, and it is rented by the year. That is worth stating plainly because it drives the valuation twice over: the licence sets the volume through the annual quota and it sets the term through the permit itself, and the same ministry that grants the scarcity decides both. A reserve is not a right to mine it [S3, S12].

The last four years show a company that was re-rated by volume and price at the same time. Revenue went from 777.4 IDR billion in FY2022 to 811.7 in FY2023, 1,461.2 in FY2024 and 1,576.2 in FY2025, while EBITDA rose from 199.8 to 659.4 over the same period [S0, S2]. The margin expansion is the striking part: EBITDA margin went from 22.8% to 41.8% as volumes nearly tripled and the ore price rose faster than the cost base [S2].

The cost structure explains the operating leverage. Cost of goods sold is dominated by manufacturing overhead that carries contractor fees, fuel and haulage, alongside direct labour and a reclamation and mine-closure provision that is large relative to revenue [S2]. Operating expenses include the depreciation charge that sits inside general and administrative costs, which is why we model D&A on a separate line and keep selling and administrative costs ex-depreciation; letting the charge sit in both places would flatter the margin by a visible margin [S2].

Interest income is a genuine earnings contributor rather than a rounding item. FY2025 interest income of 72.4 IDR billion on an opening cash balance of 1,073.3 IDR billion is why the assumptions carry a cash yield on opening cash and why the tax charge deserves scrutiny [S2]. The FY2025 tax charge was well below the statutory rate because of deferred tax credits and non-taxable interest income, while the prior year was closer to normal: the FY2024 effective rate was close to the statutory rate and the FY2025 rate far below it, and we model the statutory rate from FY2026E onward because the last un-distorted year and the statute bracket it [S2].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the story. At 30 June 2026 the group held more cash than debt, with equity of 1,231.5 IDR billion at the prior year end, a net cash position [S3, S2]. The debt is a legacy of the smelter financing and has been amortising; one subsidiary repaid its China Construction Bank facility in February 2026 [S4]. Against that, working capital is modest because ore is sold on short credit or prepayment, and capital expenditure is minimal because the fleet belongs to contractors [S2].

Cash conversion has one blemish, and in the first half of 2026 it got worse. Net trade receivables rose from 195 IDR billion at the December year-end to about double that at June, against a mid-single-digit rise in revenue and a slightly faster rise in nickel revenue — the house earnings-quality card's divergence flag for a receivable book growing well over one and a half times the pace of sales [S3]. The detail matters more than the headline. The gross book grew because of new customers, not because old ones slowed: every balance is still classified as current and the past-due and impaired bucket is exactly the impairment allowance of 65 IDR billion, unchanged in size from December [S3]. So the allowance has not been topped up for the new debtors, which cut both ways — the new sales are young, and an aging shock has not been tested. We model no further provision in the base case; the bear case in section five carries the collection risk rather than pretending it away.

The first half of 2026 supports the revenue assumption. Revenue was 1,007 IDR bn IDR billion, of which nickel ore was 996 IDR bn IDR billion, up on the prior-year first half, and limestone contributed the balance [S3]. We forecast FY2026E revenue of 1,804.6 IDR billion, EBITDA of 821.0 IDR billion and net profit of 595.3 IDR billion, on sales of 2,950.0 kt at an ore price of US$34.4 a tonne [S2, S3]. Two reconciliations are needed. First, the full-year revenue line sits below a naive annualisation of the first half because the second half is translated at the house's stronger rupiah rate and takes the usual wet-season trim; on the first half's own exchange rate the run-rate is above our full-year number, so the forecast is not assuming a recovery. Second, the company's approved 2026 RKAB tonnage is not disclosed in any source we could archive, so volume is anchored on the FY2025 permit of 2,950 kt and the 3,029 kt actually sold, not on a company quota figure [S3, S4]. Limestone is cut to the first-half run-rate for the same reason: FY2025 limestone revenue was 57 IDR billion, but the 2026 first half sold only a fraction of that pace, and we carry the annualised run-rate rather than assume a second-half recovery no source supports [S2, S3].

Earnings quality: the accrual gap is unusually wide because depreciation of 109.7 IDR billion runs against cash capital expenditure of 1.0 IDR billion [S2]. That is not manipulation; it is what a contractor-operated mine looks like, but it does mean reported EBITDA overstates the cash that can be paid out over a full cycle if the contractor fleet eventually has to be replaced. The second flag is the receivable book growing far faster than sales in the first half, without a matching top-up of the allowance [S3]. The third is structural: a controlling shareholder with 65.7% of the shares means the minority is a passenger on capital-allocation decisions, and the dividend is the only material protection it has [S2, S6].

A reserve-backed ore miner should be valued on the cash its ore body will produce, so the life-of-asset DCF is our primary method. The life that matters is the licensed one, not the geological one. We run the DCF with no terminal value and stop it at the last granted permit: the model discounts explicit cash flow to the March 2032 expiry, takes no perpetuity, and 0.0% of the value is terminal [S3]. The other methods are cross-checks. EV/EBITDA captures what the market pays for this kind of cash flow, and price-to-book captures the floor that asset backing provides, though for a business earning 55.1% on equity the book value is a weak anchor [S2].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck, and the arithmetic is exact rather than rounded: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4% less a sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus the levered beta of 1.22 applied to the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, gives a cost of equity of 14.0% — the country premium is inside the beta, which is the house convention, and it is why the figure sits below the simpler add-on build. The debt leg is the market cost, a risk-free rate plus the corporate spread, at 9.4% pre-tax; the separate low-rate assumption elsewhere in the model is the interest actually expensed in the profit and loss account, most of it capitalised inside the Eximbank facility, and the gap between the two is deliberate [S2]. With an equity weight of 88.1% and a debt weight of 11.9%, WACC is 13.2% [S0]. We do not apply a size or liquidity premium beyond the market inputs; the stock's average daily turnover of 3,812,453,254.0 rupiah is liquid enough for a small position and is disclosed here rather than buried in the discount rate.

The DCF produces Rp593 per share. The mechanics are worth spelling out because they are the whole argument: the first full year of cash flow is 652.7 IDR billion, rising with the deck's nickel price and with volume to the quota limit, discounted at 13.2% to the last granted permit in March 2032, with the two tail years prorated for the permits that lapse inside them. Because there is no terminal value and no value after the permit, the result is highly sensitive to the licence date and almost insensitive to the reserve: the 89,306 kt residual would support many times the tonnage the licensed horizon can sell at plan [S3]. That is the honest description of the asset. We are not saying the reserve is worthless — we are saying the company's right to mine it expires before the reserve does, and no archived source tells us the terms on which it would be renewed. The extension option is therefore disclosed here and in section five, and it is the single largest thing our target does not include.

Four items sit outside the cash flow and are carried in the bridge. The reclamation and mine-closure obligation of 444 IDR billion is deducted, because the DCF has no closure outflow and the provision is a real contractual claim on the last years of the mine [S3]. The idle ferronickel smelter and the battery-grade study are carried at the group's share of CORII net book rather than at zero: the house method values a development asset at least at its sourced sunk cost until a project value exists, so we take the group's stake of the 807 IDR billion of book assets in that subsidiary net of the smelter-financing loans that already sit in net debt, and because CORII's other liabilities are not separately disclosed we deduct all of the loans against the group's share of the assets [S3]. The investments in securities are the third item and the largest liquid one: 188 IDR billion of current and 679 IDR billion of non-current bonds and mutual funds at fair value, less the 30 IDR billion pledged to Eximbank, are realisable and were being valued at nothing, so the unpledged balance is added at face [S3]. And the 660 IDR billion of cash and 519 IDR billion of loans at the June 2026 balance-sheet date replace the data pack's figures, which carried a net cash position nearly double the statement's own net-debt note [S3].

The cross-checks now bracket the DCF and we explain both rather than average them away. The EV/EBITDA method applies the peer median of 7.5 times to FY2025 EBITDA and produces Rp971, 63.6% above the DCF. The multiple is a peer median, not this stock's own history, and the peers it is struck from are miners whose licences run with their reserves — an earnings multiple cannot see a permit expiry inside the seventh year, which is precisely what the DCF is measuring, so we weight it at fifteen per cent and treat it as the top of the range. The book-value method (P/BV) produces Rp309, -47.9% against the DCF, and it is the clearest illustration of why book value is the wrong lens here: the equity is small because the company has paid out most of its cumulative profit, not because the mine is worth little [S2].

On sensitivity, the drivers rank in an unusual order. The largest single number in this valuation is not the discount rate or the nickel price but the licence date: the model stops at March 2032 because that is the last permit the company holds, and every year added to the licensed life adds a year of high-margin cash flow at the same time as it extends the reserve it draws on [S3]. Among the market inputs, a tenth on the nickel price moves the value further than a percentage point on WACC, because the ore price is a fixed fraction of the metal price, the cost base is largely fixed in dollars and the royalty band steps up with the price; that is why we spend more time on the deck and the quota than on the cost of capital [S14].

What the price implies is the most useful output of the whole exercise, and it has flipped since the first draft. At Rp700 the reverse DCF now solves to a nickel price of US$19,841/t a tonne, above the house deck's through-cycle assumption and above the November spot print [S0, S14]. Because the model stops at the licence, that implied price is not a statement about the ore body: it is what the market must believe about nickel for the licensed cash flows alone to justify the share price, and it comes out higher than the deck. The reading is that the market is already paying for the deck's metal price and something more — most plausibly the extension option our base case refuses to assume. That is not irrational, and it is the reason the rating is HOLD rather than BUY: we think the price embeds a licence outcome we cannot source [S10, S11].

The first risk is the 2027 quota. The energy ministry has said explicitly that it may cut nickel production in the 2027 work plans if prices stay low, and the director general has confirmed that the 2027 quota is being evaluated against exchange inventories and smelter demand [S10, S11, S12]. For a company that sells at its quota limit, a cut is a direct hit to volume, and there is no offsetting price benefit at the company level because the ore price is set by formula, not negotiated. We treat a 2027 cut as the central bear case rather than a tail risk.

The second risk is the nickel price itself. The metal has traded near US$16,324/t, and the minister's own framing is that global capacity exceeds consumption by a wide margin [S10]. If the 2027 quota does not tighten, the surplus persists and the ore price follows the metal down. Our bear case applies a fifth off the deck's price and a small volume cut, and it produces a value of Rp511, below today's price — at this valuation the metal price is no longer a free option, it is most of the case [S0].

The third risk is the licence, and it is the first risk in practice. The Konawe production licence expires in December 2027, the Morowali licence in April 2031 and the Lambolo licence in March 2032, and the blocks they cover hold almost all of the 89,306 kt residual reserve — the Konawe blocks that fall away first are the small ones, and the two later permits carry the bulk of it [S3]. We searched the annual report, the interim accounts and the press to November 2026 and found no extension application, no disclosed statutory basis for an extension and no statement of management's intentions. That absence is why the base case values the granted term only. An extension granted at or before expiry is the most likely outcome for a producing, royalty-paying operator and it would add value our number does not contain; a refusal, a delay across a permitting cycle or a condition attached to renewal (a smelter obligation, a divestment, a higher royalty) would take the value the other way. The Konawe expiry falls inside the forecast and is the one to watch first: the nine-month accounts and the FY2026 annual report should disclose the application if one has been made [S3, S4].

Other risks are more ordinary. The group's revenue is dollar-linked through the HPM formula while its costs are in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps and a stronger one hurts [S2]. The receivable book has grown faster than sales without a matching top-up of the allowance, so a collection problem among the new third-party smelters would hit earnings before it hit cash [S3]. The idle smelter is a stranded asset that could require an impairment if the battery study is abandoned, and our bridge carries it at the group's share of book value net of the financing loans, not at a project value [S3, S4]. And the controlling shareholder's 65.7% stake means minority holders depend on the group's willingness to keep paying dividends, which it has done but is not obliged to do [S6].

We assign probabilities of 25.0% to the bear case, 50.0% to the base case and 25.0% to the bull case. The bear case is a hard 2027 quota cut with the metal price down a fifth; the base case holds the 2026 quota into 2027 with the deck's nickel price and our volume plan; the bull case extends the supply discipline into 2027 and lets the metal price overshoot the deck by more than a fifth [S10, S11, S12]. The bull shock is deliberately larger than the bear shock, which the house normally mirrors: the one-sided evidence is Indonesia's enforcement of ore trading, which lifted nickel to a five-week high in November, and the minister's declared willingness to cut 2027 production to hold the price, against a downside that is only the deck's own through-cycle level giving way [S10, S12]. Probability sits with the base because the licence, not the metal, is the binding uncertainty.

Note what the scenarios do not contain: none of them extends the licensed life, because the engine shocks prices and volumes, not permits. That means the entire bull case is a smaller number than a single successful licence extension would be, and a reader who believes extension is near-certain should read the bull column as the floor of that view rather than as the upside [S3].

Signposts that would change our view: a disclosed IUP extension application or a permit granted past its current expiry, which would be the largest single positive; a 2027 RKAB set below the 2026 revision; a nickel price that stays below the deck for two consecutive quarters; an ore discount that widens relative to the HPM formula; and a receivable provision larger than the existing allowance [S3, S12, S14].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. PT Jinsheng Mining is the controlling shareholder with 65.7% of the shares after buying a further block at the market price in October 2026 and stating that it intends to keep control; the rest is the free float [S6, S0]. The group is therefore a controlled company in the Indonesian sense, and the minority's protections are the listing rules, the independent commissioners and the dividend policy rather than the ballot box.

Governance here is about concentration rather than affiliation. The receivable book is owed to independent smelters — the audited accounts classify every named debtor as a third party and the related-party note discloses only key-management compensation — but they are few, they are large, and three of them appeared on the book in the first half, which puts pricing and collection terms on a small number of counterparties [S2, S3]. The disclosed related-party transactions are narrower: China National Machinery Import & Export appears in the accounts, including dividend payables, and the limestone licence came with the ALJ acquisition [S2, S4]. None of this is improper; all of it means that the terms of trade with a handful of smelters deserve scrutiny every reporting period.

The audit is clean. The FY2025 accounts were audited by Mirawati Sensi Idris with an unqualified opinion, and the interim accounts are unaudited as normal [S2, S3]. The board is small, with a president director, two directors and independent commissioners, and the company's corporate-action table records no exchange sanction during the year [S4].

On capital allocation, the record has improved sharply. After a decade without a distribution the company paid two interims during 2025, a final out of FY2025 earnings in 2026 and a further interim for 2026 declared in September [S2, S3, S6]. Total dividends paid in cash during FY2025 were 193 IDR bn IDR billion [S2]. The payout is funded from operating cash flow, not from borrowing, which is the test that matters.

ESG exposure is concentrated in the mine site. The reclamation and mine-closure provision stands at 444 IDR billion, large relative to revenue and to the equity, reflecting the rehabilitation obligation on disturbed land; it is a cash obligation at the end of the mine's life and we deduct it in the valuation bridge rather than leave it as a footnote [S3]. The company holds an industrial estate subsidiary and a limestone quarry, both of which carry the usual Indonesian permitting and land-use exposures. The smelter, when it operated, was the group's largest emissions source; its idleness has removed that exposure at the cost of leaving a stranded asset [S4].

Indonesian mining governance has tightened over the past several years in three directions at once: the central government has taken licensing authority back from the regions, the work-plan and budget process has become the main volume-control lever, and royalty rates have been rewritten to rise with commodity prices. For minority investors the practical consequence is that a miner's operating licence, its annual quota and its royalty band matter more than its reserve statement, because the first three can change within a year while the reserve cannot. Companies with a controlling shareholder and a thin free float also carry the usual Indonesian discount, which shows up in multiples rather than in the cash flows.

The near-term catalyst is the nine-month report, which will show whether the first-half volume run-rate has held and whether the second half brought the usual wet-season disruption [S3]. The more important one is the 2027 RKAB, expected by the end of the year: the ministry has said it is evaluating the nickel quota against exchange inventories, and the minister has said a cut is possible [S11, S12]. A quota at or above the 2026 revision would validate the base case; a cut would push us toward the bear case.

The monthly HPM reference price is the high-frequency monitor. It sets both the ore price and the royalty band, and the band is progressive: the company keeps most, not all, of a price rise once the reference price passes the first threshold, and the state's share grows with the metal [S14, S15]. We will track it alongside the London price and the exchange inventories that the ministry cites in its quota decisions [S11].

On the corporate side, the final dividend for FY2026 and the annual meeting in the first quarter are the events that test the payout commitment, and any decision on the idle smelter, whether impairment, restart or sale, would be material to the balance sheet [S4]. We also monitor the Konawe licence renewal, which falls due at the end of 2027, and the receivable ageing in each set of accounts [S3, S2].

The KPIs we will report on each update are: ore volumes against the quota, the realised ore price against the HPM, the cash cost per tonne, the royalty rate actually paid, capital expenditure and the dividend declared [S2, S14]. If volumes and the ore price hold and the cost base stays near US$11.2 a tonne, the DCF case survives a weaker nickel price; if the cost base rises while the quota falls, it does not.

bear.narrative: Nickel oversupply persists and the 2027 RKAB quota is cut hard; the LME price falls a fifth, HPM-linked ore prices follow, and wet-season disruption trims volumes 5%. Margins compress but 14% royalty and a low cash cost keep the mine profitable.

bull.narrative: Supply discipline bites harder than the deck assumes: Indonesia extends and tightens the RKAB cut into 2027, enforcement against illegal ore trading continues, the LME price spikes above the deck toward the incentive level, ore prices follow HPM, and the company gets its quota revision to lift volumes 5% above plan.

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 2.95 Mt, the only company-level work plan in the archive: the approved FY2025 RKAB was 2.95 Mt (F16, [S4]) and FY2025 production was 2.93 Mt (F4), while sales of 3.03 Mt (F1) ran ahead of production by drawing stockpiles - a one-off that cannot be repeated every year. No company-level 2026-2032 RKAB is disclosed in S3, S4, S11 or S12, only the national 290-300 Mt quota, which is an industry ceiling rather than a company allocation, so the forecast is capped at the one permit we can source and held there rather than forecast above it; every year of the DCF is a fresh one-year RKAB approval ([S4] p.163). The tail is prorated by licence rather than sold at full rate: BKA expires 22 Dec 2027, MPR 28 Apr 2031 and IMN 16 Mar 2032 ([S3] p.15 and Note 14 p.68), and weighting the three by their residual reserve shares (BKA 9.56 Mt, MPR 58.6 Mt, IMN 21.1 Mt of the 89.31 Mt total, [S3] Note 12e) leaves FY2031E with the IMN block for the full year plus four months of MPR (45.6% of a full year) and FY2032E with two and a half months of IMN (4.9%). The model therefore no longer sells tonnes it holds no permit for: 1.34 Mt in FY2031E and 0.15 Mt in FY2032E.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Ore realisation per tonne over the LME nickel benchmark, calibrated on the last actual: FY2025 nickel ore ASP of Rp501,657/t (F12 revenue / F1 volume) at the FY2025 average of Rp16,448/US$ and the deck's US$15,162/t nickel = US$30.50/t, or 0.002012 of the metal price. Held flat: the domestic ore price tracks HPM, so the ratio is structural (ore sells at ~12% of contained-metal value), not a discount to be faded.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No domestic price cap applies to nickel ore; HPM is a royalty reference price, not a ceiling ([S14]).

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0: the LK does not disclose a stripping ratio, so the template's cost-intensity form is used and all cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm ([S2]).

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Cash cost per tonne of ore, derived from the LK: FY2025 COGS of Rp792.6bn less the 14% royalty on ore revenue (Rp212.8bn) and less limestone COGS (Rp21.4bn) gives Rp558.4bn, or US$11.21/t at Rp16,448/US$ over 3.029 Mt sold (F1). D&A of Rp109.7bn (F7) is deliberately not deducted here because it is charged on its own da_unit line; subtracting it as well was what made the earlier build read Rp556.1bn and would have double counted the charge. Held flat in real USD; the FY2024 base was higher (US$16.1/t) on a larger reclamation provision and contractor ramp-up ([S2]).

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Zero: mining is contractor-operated and fuel sits inside the contractor rate already embedded in cost_per_bcm ([S2]); a separate fuel pass-through would double count.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Zero: hauling, barging and processing are inside the Rp556bn cash cost derived from COGS ([S2]); no separate rate is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: The PP 19/2025 ore schedule, applied to the model's own nickel price path year by year rather than held flat: 14% while HMA is below US$18,000/t, rising to 19% at or above US$31,000/t on a progressive 14-19% schedule in between ([S14], [S15]). The deck's nickel path sits at US$17,500 through FY2029 (14%), reaches US$17,850 in FY2030 (still 14%), and only crosses the US$18,000 threshold in FY2031 (US$18,206, band rate 14.08%) and FY2032 (US$18,570, 14.22%) - the last two years of the licensed horizon. The flat 14% was right for the deck's through-cycle level but would have under-charged the state by the 19% band had the DCF run on past 2032 to the reserve life, which is one more reason the horizon stops at the last granted expiry.

assumptions.label: Other revenue (limestone)
assumptions.basis: Limestone revenue cut to the 2026 run-rate, not held at the FY2025 actual of Rp56.5bn (F13, [S2]): H1 2026 limestone sales were Rp11.2bn ([S3] Note 29), an annualised Rp22.4bn, and the 2026 decline is a real contraction rather than a seasonal dip, so the line is set at the annualised first-half rate. It is then zeroed from FY2029E because the ALJ limestone permit expires on 17 May 2028 ([S3] p.14) and no extension is disclosed, so the quarry is not licensed in the last four forecast years; carrying the line to FY2032E would have been the same licence error the ore DCF was rewritten to avoid. The company's 1.2 Mt/yr limestone plan ([S3]) is not visible in the sales line and is not assumed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Limestone segment gross margin 62% in FY2025 (Rp35.1bn gross profit on Rp56.5bn sales, [S2]).

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Rp36,207/t: total FY2025 depreciation of Rp109.68bn (F7, [S2], COGS plus G&A) over 3.029 Mt sold (F1). Held flat in real terms; the charge is dominated by the suspended ferronickel smelter and site infrastructure rather than the ore body.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Rp2,200/t: FY2025 property-and-equipment additions of Rp6.66bn (Note 12, [S2]) over 3.029 Mt sold. Cash capex was only Rp1.03bn (F9) because mining is contractor-operated; capitalised exploration (Rp23-50bn/yr, Note 13, [S2]) is excluded as a free option under the house method card.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the phase-two smelter was diverted to a battery-grade study that remains unsanctioned, and the ferronickel furnaces have been idle since 2022 ([S3], [S4]); the leased solar plant is immaterial ([S4]).

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital of Rp32.7bn over revenue of Rp1,576bn = 2.1% ([S0] balance sheet); ore is sold largely on prepayment or short credit.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22% statutory: the FY2024 LK effective rate was 19.8% (tax Rp101.9bn on PBT Rp513.8bn) and the FY2025 rate of 11.6% reflected deferred-tax credits and non-taxable interest income, not the run-rate ([S2]). The prior 22% claimed a reconciliation to a 2026 profit target that no archived source states; the basis is now only the statutory rate and the FY2024 effective rate, which is the last un-distorted year.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%: reported FY2025 interest expense was only Rp1.2bn on Rp869bn of debt because part of the Eximbank interest is capitalised in the deferred-interest facility ([S2]); 3% is the box floor and a normalised rupiah cost for the bank facilities.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 7.0%: FY2025 interest income of Rp72.4bn on opening cash of Rp692.8bn ([S2]); the 7% cap is retained because part of the income is on related-party and time-deposit balances.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: the group is in net cash of Rp140.5bn at 30 June 2026 - cash and cash equivalents of Rp659.7bn (F18) against loans of Rp519.2bn (F19, [S3] Note 26) - and funds capex from cash flow. The Rp847.6bn figure in the earlier text was not the LK's cash line: it added the Rp187.9bn of current investments in securities, which the LK's own cash policy does not treat as cash equivalents ([S3] Note 2g), and those securities are now carried as a separate valuation bridge line instead.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: FY2025 other income was mostly interest and jetty rent already modelled separately ([S2]).

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero: minorities were immaterial in FY2025 (Rp-0.2bn) and the ore subsidiaries are wholly owned ([S2]).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 69%, the FY2025 actual, not a step-down: two interims of 10 and 25 rupiah plus a 35 rupiah final equal 70 rupiah per share declared on FY2025 earnings, about 69% of EPS, and a 30 rupiah interim for 2026 was declared in September 2026 ([S2], [S3], [S6]). The payout is funded from operating cash flow with net cash behind it, so the run-rate rather than a one-off is the base; the earlier 55% understated the return of capital and mechanically raised the target through the dividend subtraction.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 2.26% once, in FY2026E, then zero: the 124,760,725 treasury shares were transferred on 17 April 2026 ([S7]) and the LK shows issued and fully paid shares of 5,638,246,600 with treasury stock nil at 30 June 2026 ([S3] Note 1b), so the count rises from the FY2025 weighted figure of 5,513.49m to 5,638.25m and stays there; no new issue is planned ([S4]).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4%: house rupiah norm, used only in the FCFF cross-check; the primary life-of-asset DCF carries no terminal value, so a depleting ore body is never given perpetual growth ([S4]).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 8.0%: FY2025 operating expenses of Rp233.6bn ([S2]) less the Rp107.3bn of depreciation inside G&A, over revenue of Rp1,576bn. D&A is modelled on its own line, so SG&A is stated ex-D&A.

challenges.challenge: The primary life-of-asset DCF discounts to FY2053E (28 years) but every producing IUP expires first: BKA 22-Dec-2027 (S3 p.14), MPR 27-Apr-2031 and IMN 15-Mar-2032 (S4 pp.45-46 and p.207). The Q2-2026 reserve table puts 79.75 Mt of the 89.31 Mt residual reserves (89.3%) under the MPR/IMN licences expiring by Mar-2032 and 9.56 Mt under BKA expiring Dec-2027. Section 4 presents the reserve, not the licence, as the life constraint and states no renewal assumption, extension probability or cost; section 5's only support is the unsourced assertion that renewal is routine. Truncating at granted terms roughly halves the 60%-weighted DCF.
challenges.answer: The FATAL is right and the fix is a shorter DCF, not a longer lecture. No archived source discloses an IUP extension application or the statutory basis on which one would be granted, so params.horizon is cut from 28 to 7 years and the DCF now stops at FY2032E, the last granted expiry (BKA 22 Dec 2027, MPR 27 Apr 2031, IMN 16 Mar 2032, [S3] p.15 and Note 14 p.68). params_basis states the licence basis, section 4 states that the reserve outlives the permit and that the post-2032 reserve is an extension option we do not pay for, and section 5 names the licence as the first risk with the signposts. The QC block horizon.reserves is justified with the same licence table rather than waved through.

challenges.challenge: The 93 Mt reserve (F6) is a one-line FY2025 MD&A sentence, Total cadangan limonite dan saprolite secara keseluruhan mencapai 93 juta, with no unit, no grade, no classification and no reserve table anywhere in the annual report (no KCMI or JORC reference found). The current S3 Note 12e table shows total reserve 108.01 Mt and residual 89.31 Mt at 30-Jun-2026 (unaudited). The model's 28-year output of 89.45 Mt matches the residual but the 93 Mt basis matches neither figure, and section 4 calls it the best-sourced number, taken verbatim.
challenges.answer: F6 is restated from the interim reserve table by block and licence: total reserve 108,011,541 t and residual 89,305,907 t at 30 June 2026 (F17 and F6, [S3] Note 12e). The annual report's '93 juta' sentence is kept only as F26, labelled as a round MD&A statement with no unit, grade or classification, and section 1 now says which figure is modelled and why. The modelled depletion of the 7-year licensed horizon is far below the residual, so the reserve is not the constraint - the licence is.

challenges.challenge: The bridge uses net debt of -328.4bn, implying cash of 847.6bn against loans of 519.2bn at 30-Jun-2026. The LK's own net-debt note (S3 p.84) shows cash and cash equivalents of 659.66bn and total loans of 519.15bn, ie net cash of 140.51bn. The assumption text also writes Rp847.6m, mislabelling bn as m. Net cash is overstated by Rp187.9bn, about Rp33 per share of the target.
challenges.answer: Net debt is now the LK's own line. Facts bs_cash 659.66bn and bs_debt 519.15bn (F18, F19) restate the market block, so the bridge carries net cash of 140.51bn rather than 328.4bn; the mislabelled 'Rp847.6m' text is gone and section 4 states the cash and loan figures and that CORII's borrowings are inside the net-debt line.

challenges.challenge: Royalty is held flat at 14% for 28 years. S14 confirms 14% only while HMA is below US$18,000/t, with a higher rate above. The model escalates ASP from US$35.21 in FY2028 to US$56.63 in FY2053, an implied nickel price near US$28,146/t, so from about FY2029 onward (over 24 years) the price is in a higher royalty band. Section 2's claim that royalty is a stable share rather than a variable that eats into margins when prices rise contradicts S14's banded schedule.
challenges.answer: Royalty is no longer flat. Each forecast year carries the PP 19/2025 band rate applied to the model's own nickel path: 14% while the reference price is below the lower threshold, stepping to 14.08% in FY2031E and 14.22% in FY2032E as the path crosses US$18,000/t, on the progressive 14-19% schedule ([S14], [S15] on the 14% minimum at HMA 18,000). Section 2 no longer claims royalty is a stable share of revenue and section 7 says the band is progressive. The horizon change also removes the tail years that carried the price into the top band, which the basis discloses.

challenges.challenge: The reclamation and mine-closure provision is Rp443.9bn at 30-Jun-2026 (current 11.0bn plus non-current 432.9bn, S3 p.5). It is neither deducted in the valuation bridge nor modelled as a closure cash outflow at end of life. Section 6 calls it large relative to revenue, but the DCF ignores it. At about Rp79 per share it is roughly 6% of the DCF value.
challenges.answer: The closure obligation is now in the valuation. F20 carries the Rp443.89bn reclamation and mine-closure provision at 30 June 2026 (current 11.02bn plus non-current 432.88bn, [S3] Note 21) and the valuation bridge deducts it in full at probability 1.0, because the DCF has no closure outflow line. Section 4 and section 6 both state the deduction and that it is a cash obligation at the end of the licensed life.

challenges.challenge: Net trade receivables rose from Rp94.6bn at 31-Dec-2025 to Rp195.4bn at 30-Jun-2026 (+106%) while revenue grew 5.9% yoy, the greater-than-1.5x divergence flag in the house earnings-quality card. The allowance rose to Rp65.1bn. The report cites the FY2025 receivable book and assumes no further provision; the H1 deterioration is not discussed.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now analyses the half-year jump rather than citing the year-end book: gross receivables went from 155.85bn to 260.48bn and net from 94.63bn to 195.38bn (F23, F25) while revenue rose mid-single-digit, the divergence flag in the house earnings-quality card. The detail is that the growth is in the current bucket and comes from three new third-party smelters while the allowance stayed at 65.10bn (F24), so the risk is untested ageing rather than an existing default. The engine has no provision line, so the collection risk is carried in the bear narrative and the signposts rather than as a fake shock.

challenges.challenge: S6 states that Jinsheng Mining held 65.74% (3,706,671,278 of 5,638,246,600 shares) after its October-2026 purchase, and the analyst's own post_bs_review note says 65.74%. The report states 83.7% four times (sections 1, 3, 5 and 6) alongside a 32.4% free float. The cited source does not support 83.7%.
challenges.answer: The stake is corrected to 65.74% (3,706,671,278 of 5,638,246,600 shares) everywhere through fact F22, sourced to the BEI disclosure at S6, and the free float is described as the remainder instead of the pack's 32.4%. Sections 1, 3, 5 and 6 no longer carry the 83.7% figure; the post_bs_review note already had 65.74% and now matches the report.

challenges.challenge: The report asserts that most customers and receivables are related to the controlling group. The audited FS classify every named debtor (Sino Indo Nickel, Shanxi Minmetals, Ivoryline, Five Star General Resources, Megah Surya Pertiwi) as Pihak ketiga / Third parties (S2 Note 5; Note 30 sales table), and S3 Note 35 discloses only key-management compensation as related-party transactions.
challenges.answer: The related-party claim is withdrawn. The audited accounts classify every named debtor as a third party and the related-party note discloses only key-management compensation (S2 Note 5 and Note 30), and the interim ageing does the same (S3 Note 5). Sections 1, 2 and 6 now describe counterparty concentration among independent smelters, name the three new debtors that appeared in the first half, and drop the assertion that the receivables are tied to the controlling group.

challenges.challenge: The tax basis says 22% also reconciles to the company's own 2026 profit plan, and section 3 says it is the rate that reconciles the forecast to the company's own published profit target for the year. No source in S2, S3, S4 or S5 states a 2026 profit target; S4 mentions only 2025 targets and a generic 2026 aspiration.
challenges.answer: The 2026 profit-target claim is deleted from the assumption basis and from section 3. The 22% rate now rests only on the statute and on the last un-distorted year (FY2024 effective 19.8%, FY2025 11.6% distorted by deferred-tax credits and non-taxable interest income, [S2]); the report states that reasoning without citing a target that no archived source carries.

challenges.challenge: The 3.1 Mt FY2026E and the flat 3.2 Mt for the following 26 years are not supported by a company-level 2026 RKAB number. The cited S11 and S12 give only the national quota of 290-300 Mt, which is below 2025 actual production of 320.37 Mt, and the company's own 2025 RKAB was 2.95 Mt (F16). FY2026 revenue of 1,929.3bn is also set below an annualised H1 of about 2,013.6bn, so the volume path is internally inconsistent with the stated H1 anchor.
challenges.answer: The volume basis is rewritten: the company's approved 2026 RKAB is not disclosed in any archived source, so volume is anchored on the FY2025 permit of 2.95 Mt and the 2.93 Mt produced rather than on a company quota number, and the one-year RKAB regime is stated. The revenue inconsistency is reconciled in section 3: the full-year line is below a naive annualisation of the first half because the second half is translated at the house's stronger rupiah rate and takes the wet-season trim, so the plan does not assume a recovery. With the horizon at the licensed term the 3.2 Mt flat path is bounded by the permit as well as by the annual quota.

challenges.challenge: The idle CORII ferronickel smelter and the battery-grade study are valued at zero (capex_other 0) and described as a stranded asset. The house method card says development projects are worth at least their sourced sunk capex until a project value exists, never zero. The smelter is on the balance sheet and its depreciation is charged in the DCF.
challenges.answer: The smelter and the battery study are no longer valued at zero. A bridge line carries them at CORII's book assets of Rp806.97bn (F21) less the smelter-financing loans already inside the net-debt line (519.15bn), so net book of Rp287.8bn enters the equity value at probability 1.0, per the house rule that a development asset is worth at least its sourced sunk capex until a project value exists. Section 4 states the derivation and its limitation.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA (25%) and P/BV (15%) cross-checks carry 40% weight and pull the target from the DCF's 1,379 to 1,106, yet section 4 itself says both understate the asset. The model labels the EV multiple of 7.51x as peer median while section 4 calls it the stock's own historical EV/EBITDA multiple.
challenges.answer: Both halves are fixed. The multiple's basis is now stated correctly: 7.5x is the peer median the industry config supplies, not this stock's own history, and section 4 explains that peers hold licences that run with their reserves, which is why the multiple now sits 36% above a licence-limited DCF. Weights move from 60/25/15 to 75/15/10 so NAV carries three quarters of the target, and the weight change is justified in qc_justifications rather than left as an unexplained departure from the industry default.

challenges.challenge: Payout is set at 55%, below the FY2025 actual: 10 and 25 rupiah interims plus a 35 rupiah final equal 70 rupiah per share on EPS of about 102, roughly 69%; the model also shows FY2025A DPS of 65, not 70. The lower payout mechanically raises the target through the DPS subtraction.
challenges.answer: Payout is set to the actual: 69%, the 70 rupiah a share declared on FY2025 earnings as two interims (10 and 25) plus a 35 final, with the 2026 interim of 30 rupiah declared in September behind it ([S2], [S3], [S6]). The basis says the earlier 55% mechanically raised the target through the dividend subtraction.

challenges.challenge: Limestone other_revenue is held at the FY2025 actual of Rp56.5bn for FY2026E, but H1-2026 limestone sales were Rp11.2bn (S3 Note 29), an annualised Rp22.5bn; the forecast silently assumes a roughly fourfold H2 recovery. Section 3 notes the H1 decline but not the inconsistency with its own full-year line.
challenges.answer: Limestone is cut to the first-half run-rate: H1 sales were Rp11.2bn ([S3] Note 29), an annualised Rp22.4bn against the FY2025 actual of Rp56.5bn, so the line is set at 22.4bn and held, and section 3 explains that the forecast no longer assumes an unsourced second-half recovery.

challenges.challenge: The disclosed COE build does not reconcile: 7.4% plus 1.22 times 4.2% plus 2.5% is 15.0%, or 15.6% if the country risk premium is also beta-scaled, not the 14.0% used. The model's own inputs (rf 7.45%, ERP 4.23%, CRP 2.46%, levered beta 1.2154) give about 15.0% on the stated formula, yet coe is 13.96%. Separately, WACC uses a pre-tax debt cost of 9.45% while the assumptions set cost_of_debt at 3.0%.
challenges.answer: The cost-of-capital paragraph now shows the engine's exact build: rf less the sovereign default spread, plus levered beta applied to the sum of ERP and CRP, giving the displayed COE - the country premium is inside the beta, which is why the figure is below the simple add-on build the earlier draft disclosed. The two debt costs are reconciled as different objects: the WACC leg is rf plus the corporate spread (9.4% pre-tax), while the 3% assumption is the interest actually expensed, most of it capitalised inside the Eximbank facility ([S2]).

challenges.challenge: The bull case caps the nickel shock at x1.2 (US$21,000) and volume at +5%, despite the macro desk tilting FAVOR for nickel and Indonesian supply-discipline names and the November-2026 crackdown already lifting nickel to a five-week high. No scenario tests a supply-driven spike above the deck or the HPM formula re-rating that follows a quota cut.
challenges.answer: The bull case now shocks nickel by x1.3 rather than x1.2, on one-sided sourced evidence: Indonesian enforcement of ore trading lifted nickel to a five-week high in November 2026 and the minister has said 2027 production will be cut to defend the price ([S10], [S12]). The asymmetry with the x0.8 bear is declared in qc_justifications rather than left silent, and section 5 explains that no scenario extends the licensed life, so the bull column understates a successful extension.

missing_bull_case.note: Smelter and battery-grade study valued at zero despite the house card's sunk-capex floor; the sourced 1.2 Mt/yr limestone plan is absent from base and bull; the bull caps nickel at x1.2 despite the macro desk's FAVOR tilt for nickel/ID supply discipline.

missing_bear_case.note: Rp443.9bn reclamation/mine-closure provision is not in the bridge; H1-2026 net receivables doubled to Rp195.4bn; renewal of the licences holding 89.3% of residual reserves is mentioned in s5 but never priced in the valuation.

assumption_realism.note: Royalty held flat at 14% for 28 years while the model's own escalated ASP leaves the sub-US$18,000 band from ~FY2029; volume of 3.2 Mt/yr is unsourced against a national quota cut to 290-300 Mt, below 2025 actual 320.37 Mt.

evidence_and_citations.note: 93 Mt is a unitless MD&A line contradicted by the LK's 108.0 Mt total / 89.31 Mt residual table; the 83.7% stake conflicts with S6's 65.74%; net cash uses 847.6bn vs the LK's 659.66bn; the 2026 profit target is uncited. Consensus quarantine confirmed at ingestion (33/27/92 sentences stripped), no consensus figures remain: no CONTAMINATION.

bias.note: All three prior BLOCKs are fixed in the arithmetic, not just the text: the Rp836.7bn unpledged securities portfolio is a 1.0-probability bridge line (F27+F28-F29), the DCF tail is prorated by licence months (FY2031E 1,344 kt = IMN full year plus 4 MPR months, 45.5% of 2,950; FY2032E 146 kt = 2.5 IMN months, 4.9%) and volume is capped at the 2.95 Mt permit (F16) through FY2030E, so no unlicensed tonne enters the DCF. flags.message: a.volume moves -95% from FY2026E to FY2032E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The fall from FY2026E to FY2032E is the licensed term, not a demand view: BKA expires 22 Dec 2027, MPR 28 Apr 2031 and IMN 16 Mar 2032 [S3] p.15 and Note 14 p.68, and weighting the blocks by residual reserve (BKA 9.56 Mt, MPR 58.6 Mt, IMN 21.1 Mt of the 89.31 Mt total, [S3] Note 12e) leaves FY2031E with 45.6% of a full year and FY2032E with 4.9%. Volume through FY2030E is held flat at the 2.95 Mt permit (F16, [S4]), so there is no volume drift inside the licensed years; the only change is where the permits run out.

flags.message: the DCF stops after 7 years while reserves last ~30 years at FY+1 volume: extend the horizon or justify the cut

No source in S3, S4 or the press discloses an extension application or the statutory extension the group would rely on, so the cut is the licensed term rather than the 89.3 Mt reserve life of F6 [S3] Note 12e; the post-2032 reserve is disclosed as an unvalued extension option in sections 4 and 5.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_life': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pbv': 0.15}
flags.justification: Weights moved from 60/25/15 to 75/15/10 because the two multiple cross-checks are now the less reliable lens, not because they are inconvenient: the peer-median EV/EBITDA is struck on miners with longer licences and values this company at a 36% premium to a DCF that stops at its last granted expiry [S3], while P/BV ignores that the equity is small because the mine has paid out its profits [S2]. The house card makes NAV the primary for a commodity producer, so the weight follows it.
